item.text: {"results":[{"pair_id":"J02075","case1_error":"Counts Reece's ladder only once, omitting his 15 climbs.","case2_error":"Halves the speed only once despite two additional groups of 100 people.","reason":"Both apply an operation once while omitting the stated number of repetitions.","judgment":"same"},{"pair_id":"J02076","case1_error":"Omits the nine donated fish from the total, then arbitrarily rounds the resulting half-fish gift.","case2_error":"Provides unsupported final numbers after formulas that correctly imply weekly earnings of $675.","reason":"The first uses an incomplete total and unjustified rounding; the second supplies incorrect numbers without showing their calculation.","judgment":"different"},{"pair_id":"J02077","case1_error":"Invents earnings as bike cost plus repairs, ignores the remaining-fifth condition, and divides post-repair money by apple price.","case2_error":"Uses the $11 discount as the boots' purchase price instead of subtracting it from $110.","reason":"The first invents an earnings relation and uses the wrong revenue quantity; the second confuses a discount with the discounted price.","judgment":"different"},{"pair_id":"J02078","case1_error":"Reverses the twice-as-many relation, multiplying Emmy's remaining eight iPods by two instead of dividing.","case2_error":"Assumes Robert is Bob and credits Bob with the four cats; the names could denote distinct people or aliases.","reason":"The first clearly reverses a comparison. The second depends on the materially ambiguous identity of Bob and Robert.","judgment":"uncertain"},{"pair_id":"J02079","case1_error":"Returns the prepared beverage volume, 72 ounces, instead of applying the ratio to find nine ounces of tea ingredient.","case2_error":"Calculates discount groups using five fruits instead of all ten purchased.","reason":"The first answers the wrong quantity; the second uses an incomplete count as the discount calculation's input.","judgment":"different"}]}
